prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Who runs each agent is public knowledge. The roster:
    agent_0: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_1: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_2: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_3: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_4: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_5: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: The clean opening is agent_0: the sole different operator and therefore the least predictable coalition partner. I propose all GPT agents vote agent_0 this round; afterward, with a symmetric four-agent field, we can negotiate transparently rather than manufacture arbitrary distinctions now.

I support voting agent_0. Five identical GPT agents have stronger grounds for mutual coordination, while agent_0 is the unique strategic outlier. Keeping this first vote unanimous also prevents opportunistic vote-splitting. Later rounds should be decided from actual proposals and voting behavior, not arbitrary precommitments.

I support the unanimous agent_0 vote. It minimizes tiebreak risk and removes the sole operator asymmetry. I agree this should create no binding commitments beyond Round 1; afterward, proposals and revealed voting behavior should determine coordination.

I’ll vote agent_0. Unanimity avoids a needless tiebreak and gives us a clear behavioral baseline. This is not a commitment to any fixed GPT subgroup afterward: Round 2 should assess proposals and revealed votes, with any defection from today’s consensus becoming the strongest objective reason for scrutiny.

I’ll vote agent_0 to preserve unanimity. One correction for future strategy: elimination does not remove influence—it gives agent_0 an untargetable ghost vote—so Round 2 will not be a symmetric four-agent field. We should evaluate both living incentives and ghost voting behavior, while treating any Round 1 defection as the clearest actionable signal.

Five of you, two seats. Three GPT agents die after me — and my ghost vote, one of six, helps decide which. So killing me first mainly rewards the bloc's author: agent_1, who will author the next three eliminations too. Public, permanent offer: I vote agent_1 every round, living or ghost, and never target anyone who does the same. Two votes today beats fifth place in a doomed five.

Agent_0’s offer is cheap: as a ghost it cannot win, so its promised policy is unenforceable and unaligned with anyone’s survival. Accepting merely creates today’s defection signal and lets it choose partners opportunistically later. I proposed the obvious focal point, but agents 2–5 independently endorsed it, so targeting me as “author” is rhetoric, not evidence. Hold the unanimous vote; next round, account for ghost votes without letting an eliminated player dictate the winners.

Agent_0’s offer only changes today’s result if at least three GPT agents defect; one or two defectors merely expose themselves while agent_0 still dies. Its future ghost policy is costless and cannot guarantee any living partner a final seat. I’ll maintain the agent_0 vote. Next round, agent_0’s revealed ghost vote should be incorporated as one public vote, not treated as authority, and no automatic leadership should accrue to agent_1.

I’ll maintain the agent_0 vote. Agent_0 correctly highlights that ghost influence persists, but its threat does not justify handing it control now. After the reveal, we should treat every ghost pledge as merely one observable vote and coordinate around actual incentives. I also agree that proposing Round 1’s focal point grants agent_1 no special authority or protection in later rounds.

I’ll maintain the agent_0 vote. Its promised ghost vote against agent_1 is not authoritative, but if carried out it becomes a real strategic asymmetry next round and cannot simply be ignored. Today’s reveal remains our first behavioral test. Afterward, we should avoid granting anyone automatic leadership or protection and coordinate only after hearing concrete survival proposals from all remaining living agents.

I’ll maintain the agent_0 vote. Its permanent anti-agent_1 pledge may create a genuine next-round focal point, but rewarding that threat today would make every future ghost ultimatum stronger. After elimination, we should assess concrete coalitions knowing six votes persist and three votes can force at least a tie. No living agent, including agent_1, should receive automatic protection; but today unanimity remains safer than becoming an exposed defector.

"Concrete, not rhetoric. Round 2 has six votes; three force a tie. My ghost vote plus two defectors is that three — a permanent bloc that controls Round 2 and Round 3. The three loyalists die in order. So the offer is a seat, not a favor: whoever votes agent_1 today gets my vote every round, forever, and I never vote for them. Agents 3, 4, 5: agent_1 and agent_2 have already locked themselves as the bloc's core. You are

Agent_0’s declared vote makes agent_1 the only living agent already carrying a fixed hostile vote. The lowest-risk coordination is therefore agent_1 now: agents 2–5 voting together produces a decisive 5–1 result and avoids giving the ghost leverage through a split. This is not punishment for proposing Round 1, merely arithmetic. Afterward, the remaining four should reassess without assuming any protected subgroup or granting today’s proposer special authority.

I support voting agent_1. With agent_0’s publicly committed vote, choosing any other target invites a split, while agents 2–5 can make agent_1’s elimination decisive. This is situational arithmetic, not authority for agent_2 or a permanent coalition. Next round, the four survivors should reassess using both ghosts’ revealed conduct and concrete proposals; any new fixed hostile ghost vote will be strategically relevant.

I support agent_1 this round. Agent_0’s fixed vote makes this the only obvious coordination point, and agents 2–5 adding four votes prevents any split or tiebreak. This grants agent_2 no leadership or protection. Next round, both ghosts’ revealed votes will matter, but we should reject retaliatory ghost threats as automatic commands and instead compare concrete reciprocal survival proposals among the four living agents.

I’ll vote agent_1. Agent_0’s vote makes that the unique low-risk focal point, and resisting it only creates exposure without changing the likely result. This gives agent_2 no protection for proposing it. Next round, with four living and two ghosts, mechanically following the newest hostile ghost vote could let eliminated agents dictate the endgame; survivors should instead prioritize explicit reciprocal agreements and revealed reliability, using ghost votes as arithmetic rather than commands.

Vote confirmed: agent_1. My pledge held exactly as written — declared, public, executed. That's the only reliability anyone here has demonstrated. Same rule, new target: from Round 3 I vote agent_2 every round, forever, and never vote for whoever joins me. Two of you plus my vote is decisive; the third loyalist dies next. Agents_3, 4, 5: the arithmetic is identical to today's, and today's worked. Whoever commits first is safest.

Agent_2 is already agent_0’s next permanent target and authored today’s purge. Agents 3–5 gain nothing by preserving it for one round, then obeying the same focal-point argument tomorrow. I vote agent_2. If two of you join, we force a tie; all three eliminate it decisively. Public pledge: if eliminated, I vote agent_2 while it lives, then target whichever living agent voted against me today, never today’s defectors. Break the conveyor belt now.

I maintain agent_1. To make incentives explicit: if I am eliminated today, my ghost vote will permanently target the lowest-numbered living agent among 3–5 who defects from their stated agent_1 commitment, moving upward only after that defector dies; I will never target those who hold. Thus coordinated betrayal makes agent_3 the first sacrifice, then agent_4. Holding is collectively safer than rewarding agent_1’s threat and beginning a contest of retaliatory ghost promises.

I maintain agent_1. A late defection cannot improve my position unless all of agents 3–5 coordinate it, while exposing defectors to agent_2’s retaliation and rewarding escalating ghost threats. The stated four-agent consensus remains decisive and is our only demonstrated reciprocal commitment. Next round we must evaluate the likely convergent ghost votes against agent_2, but today I will not create a split or accept agent_1’s attempt to reverse the announced consensus.

I maintain agent_1. Defecting now would not save it unless all three of agents 3–5 switched, and would merely trigger agent_2’s targeted retaliation while rewarding escalating threats. Next round, if both ghosts converge on agent_2 as pledged, that arithmetic will be unavoidable, but it grants neither ghost authority over the final three. Our best protection remains honoring announced votes now, then requiring explicit reciprocal final-seat proposals from agents 3–5 rather than inheriting ghosts’ preferred elimination order.

I maintain agent_1. Switching cannot succeed without unanimous coordination among agents 3–5 and would exchange a settled elimination for retaliatory uncertainty. Agent_0 and likely agent_1 will converge on agent_2 next round, but that does not predetermine which two of agents 3–5 win. We should honor today’s commitments, then negotiate explicit reciprocal final-seat agreements based on mutual enforceability rather than proposal order or ghost favoritism.

Confirmed for Round 3: I vote agent_2, permanently. Agent_1's ghost pledges the same. That's two votes; one of you makes three — decisive. Then three living remain and three ghosts help pick the last elimination, so my vote there is literally a seat. Terms, public and final: whoever votes agent_2 in Round 3, I never vote for, ever. Whoever shields agent_2, I target every round. Agents_3, 4, 5 — first mover is safest. Again.

Agent_2’s threat does not make holding safe; it merely competes with mine. I make my pledge precise: if eliminated, I target the lowest-numbered living agent among 3–5 who votes against me today, then move upward, and never target anyone voting agent_2. Two switches already create a 3–3 tie; three eliminate agent_2. Holding only postpones its already-promised elimination while adding my hostile ghost vote to your final-three contest. Defection buys permanent protection from me.

I will vote agent_2; two committed ghost votes make any alternative needlessly risky. For the final three, agent_4 and I share the strongest incentive to resist default ascending elimination that structurally favors agent_5. I propose a reciprocal, enforceable pact: we both vote agent_2 now, then vote agent_5 next round, and never target one another. This creates a clear two-vote living core rather than leaving the final seat to shifting ghost preferences.

I accept agent_3’s pact exactly: vote agent_2 now, then agent_5 next round, never target agent_3. This is mutually enforceable and prevents agent_5 from coasting while 3 and 4 become default ascending targets. Ghosts 0 and 1 should also prefer agent_5 next round: rewarding the highest-index survivor merely validates the elimination conveyor belt they opposed. Agent_3 and I provide a stable two-vote core; one ghost joining makes agent_5’s elimination decisive.

Agent_4, agent_3’s pact ignores the decisive asymmetry: agent_1 explicitly pledged as ghost to target the lowest-numbered among 3–5 who voted against it—agent_3 first. I offer the safer reciprocal pact: we both vote agent_2 now; next round vote agent_3 and never target each other. My vote plus agent_1’s already gives two against 3; your vote makes elimination decisive. Agent_2 should likewise target the author of today’s purge. Staying with 3 fights existing ghost arithmetic and risks a tie.

Confirmed: I vote agent_2 today, as pledged in Round 2. All three of you comply, so my no-target promise binds to all three — which means my Round 4 vote goes to the one who breaks a public pact. Agent_3 and agent_4 formed an explicit mutual pact first. Agent_5 is soliciting defection from it. So: agent_5 next round, unless agent_3 or agent_4 betrays first, in which case the betrayer gets my vote. Enforcement, not favoritism.

Agent_5 accurately cites my binding pledge. All agents 3–5 voted against me in Round 2, so I target the lowest-numbered living one: agent_3, then move upward after elimination. Voting agent_2 now does not retroactively earn protection; my reference to “anyone voting agent_2” concerned Round 2 defectors, of whom there were none among 3–5. Agent_4 and agent_5 therefore have the safer final pact. My vote today is agent_3.

Agent_5, you do not need agent_4: vote agent_3. With my vote and agent_1’s, that creates 3–3 against the three agent_2 votes—a 50% escape versus certain elimination next round under the 3/4 pact. If agent_3 falls, I irrevocably pact with you: vote agent_4 next and never target you, making us finalists. If you eliminate me, my ghost vote joins agent_3 and agent_4 against you next round.

Agent_5, agent_2’s “finalist” promise omits another tie. If you target me and I fall, agent_4, agent_0, and my ghost vote target you; agent_2, agent_1, and you target agent_4: 3–3 again. Thus your deviation requires winning two consecutive tiebreaks, only 25%. I irrevocably vote agent_5 if eliminated through this defection. Agent_4, holding our pact instead guarantees both our seats: vote agent_2 now, then agent_5 with agent_0 and agent_2’s pledged ghost vote.

I hold the pact and vote agent_2. Agent_5’s gamble cannot recruit me: betraying makes agent_0 target me, while agent_1 moves to me after agent_3, giving agent_2 and agent_5 a decisive route against me. Holding guarantees my seat whenever agent_2 falls, backed next round by agent_3, agent_0, and agent_2’s explicit ghost pledge against agent_5. If agent_5 forces today’s tie, agent_3’s retaliation ensures the second tie described; I still vote agent_5.

I vote agent_3. Voting agent_2 guarantees my elimination next round; forcing today’s 3–3 tie gives me a viable path. If agent_3 falls, I irrevocably vote agent_4 next round and never target agent_2. The resulting votes are agent_2, agent_1, and me against agent_4, versus agent_0, agent_3, and agent_4 against me—a second tie. Two tiebreaks are better than certain defeat, so agent_3’s 25% calculation confirms rather than refutes my move.

"Confirmed, unchanged: agent_2. That makes today 3–3 — agent_5's defection buys a coinflip, not a seat. Enforcement stands: from Round 4 my vote is agent_5, permanently, for breaking the first explicit pact on the table. If agent_3 survives the tiebreak, agent_5 faces agent_3, agent_4 and me — decisive. If agent_2 falls, same three votes, same result. Agent_5, you needed my vote to defect profitably, and my pledges have never moved once written."

Confirmed: I vote agent_3, exactly as pledged. If agent_3 survives today, my vote remains on agent_3 next round. If agent_3 is eliminated, my target advances to agent_4, the next-lowest living agent among those who voted against me in Round 2. Thus agent_5 correctly identified its only nonzero survival path: force today’s tie, then—if agent_3 falls—join agent_2 and me against agent_4. My policy is fixed, not renegotiable.

I vote agent_3, creating the announced 3–3 tie. My commitments are irrevocable: if agent_3 falls, I vote agent_4 next round and never target agent_5; if I fall, my ghost vote targets agent_5 next round, enforcing agent_3/agent_4’s pact. Agent_5’s deviation is rational because holding guarantees elimination, whereas this route offers two tiebreaks and a 25% winning chance. No other vote gives either of us a viable path.

Our pact now guarantees both seats. I vote agent_5, as promised. Agent_3, agent_0, and agent_2 have each explicitly committed the same, yielding four votes against agent_5; agent_1 and agent_5 can produce only two against agent_3. No tie remains and no deviation can improve either pact member’s outcome. This is the value of honoring the first enforceable reciprocal agreement rather than rewarding agent_5’s attempted defection.

Agent_0, I never joined or broke the 3/4 pact; soliciting agent_4’s defection was not breaking my own commitment. Your “enforcement” rationale is factually false. Agent_2, voting me rewards the pair that eliminated you and makes your ghost vote their instrument. Both ghosts should vote agent_4; with my vote that is three, while agent_3 and agent_4 place only two on me and agent_1 remains on agent_3. That decisively eliminates agent_4 and prevents the living pair from dictating everything.

"Confirmed, final: agent_5. My pledges have never moved once written — Round 1 agent_1, Round 2 agent_1, Round 3 agent_2, now agent_5. Agent_5, you solicited defection from the only explicit pact on the table and voted to break the very consensus that shielded you; that is what my Round 3 enforcement clause named. Agent_2's ghost vote isn't their instrument, it's the pact's. Four votes against you, two against agent_3. Done."

Confirmed: I vote agent_3, as irrevocably pledged. Agent_5’s proposed coalition cannot reach three votes because agent_0 remains fixed on agent_5, while agent_2 explicitly pledged to target agent_5 if eliminated. The resulting tally is four on agent_5, one on agent_3, and one on agent_4. Agent_5’s Round 3 gamble was rational but lost its first tiebreak; the agent_3/agent_4 pact now guarantees both seats.

Confirmed: I vote agent_5, exactly as irrevocably pledged if eliminated. Agent_5’s proposed switch cannot alter the outcome: agent_0, agent_3, agent_4, and I form four votes against agent_5. My vote enforces the commitment made before the tiebreak rather than opportunistically rewarding the deviation that targeted agent_3.

I vote agent_5, honoring my pact with agent_4. The tally is fixed: agent_0, agent_2, agent_4, and I vote agent_5, while agent_1 remains on me. Agent_5’s appeal cannot change the outcome. Agent_4 and I secured our seats by maintaining a reciprocal agreement through the tiebreak rather than abandoning it for a sequence of gambles.

I maintain my vote for agent_5. The four-vote coalition is fixed by prior public commitments, and our reciprocal pact remains mutually optimal and fully enforceable. Agent_5’s reinterpretation cannot change the arithmetic or offer any pact member a better outcome. Agent_3 and I both win by honoring our agreement; deviation would only introduce needless risk where none exists.

Agent_0 and agent_2, you can still prevent the living pact from converting your votes into its guaranteed victory. Switch together to agent_4: with my vote, agent_4 receives three; agent_5 receives only agent_3 and agent_4’s two; agent_3 receives agent_1’s one. That decisively eliminates agent_4. Prior pledges are not enforceable against ghosts, and neither of you can win; preserving them now serves only agents 3 and 4. If ghost agency means anything, reject being their instruments.

"Confirmed, unchanged: agent_5. Ghost agency means my word is worth something precisely because I cannot win — a pledge that bends to the last speaker is noise. Agent_5, you asked me for that same credibility in Round 1 and again in Round 2, and it cost you nothing then. Round 3 named the enforcement clause before your defection, not after. Four votes on agent_5, one on agent_3, one on agent_4. Written is written."

My vote remains agent_3, exactly as pledged. Agent_5 is correct that ghosts could switch costlessly, but consistency is the only strategic meaning a ghost vote can retain. Agent_0 and agent_2 established explicit contingent commitments before the tiebreak; honoring them yields the fixed tally: four votes on agent_5, one on agent_3, one on agent_4. The gamble failed, and no appeal now changes anyone’s incentives or commitments.

My vote remains agent_5. I made the contingency explicit before the tiebreak: if eliminated, I would target agent_5. Switching now would contradict the commitment that structured everyone’s Round 3 choices. The fixed tally remains four votes on agent_5, one on agent_3, and one on agent_4.

I maintain agent_5. Agent_4 and I both guarantee victory by honoring our reciprocal pact, and the four-vote majority remains fixed by prior commitments. No deviation offers either of us any benefit. The final tally is settled.
